## 3.10 Answers

### Question 2

```{r}
exercise_counts <- c(100, 233, 41, 232, 656, 12, 92)

mean(exercise_counts)
```

The first chunk does not give any errors, it correctly calculates the mean of the given vector of numbers.

```{r}
exercise_counts <- c(100, 233, 41, 232, "656", 12, 92)

mean(exercise_counts)
```

The second chunk doesn't give an error, but a warning. It clearly hasn't returned the result we wanted. The reason for this is that our vector of numbers contains a variable of the **character** type, which is not numeric. This has changed the whole vector into a **character** vector. The `mean()` function requires either **numeric** or **logical** inputs, and as soon as a single input is not either of those, it returns `NA`. (As an aside, you might try replacing "656" with FALSE, and see what happens...and have a think why!)

```{r}
#| error: true
#| 
exercise_counts <- c(100, 233, 41, 232, 656, 12, 92)

mean(exercise_count)
```

This third chunk does give an error. This is a classic example of *R* taking us literally—we have a typo in the `mean()` function where we have asked it to take the mean of an object that doesn't exist (missing an 's' from the name). *R* doesn't know that it was just a typo and won't fix it for us.

my_median
my_variance
my_SD

### Question 4

```{r}
new_vector <- c(141, 61, 883, 548, 981, NA, 23)

mean(new_vector)

```

This is similar to what happens if there is the wrong variable type for the `mean()` function to work. Any `NA`s in the input lead to the output just being `NA`, because *R* cannot determine the mean of a vector if there is a missing value.

### Question 5

```{r}

mean(new_vector, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The `na.rm` argument allows the `NA` value to be ignored when calculating the mean. It isn't a "one-size-fits-all" fix though. It is still important to have a strategy for identifying and handling missing values in data.

## 5.8 Answers

### Question 1

```{r}
results |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100) +
  labs(
    x = "log2 fold change (TBI vs sham)",
    y = "Number of genes"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

A tall symmetrical peak centred on zero, with long thin tails. Most genes don't change at all—which is exactly what you should expect, and what the boxplot in Plot 3 was telling you. The interesting biology lives in those tails.

### Question 2

```{r}
results <- results |> 
  mutate(
    significant = !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05 & abs(log2FoldChange) > 1
  )
```

Then the plot code should work without changing anything:

```{r}
#| echo: false
newvolcano <- results |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), colour = significant)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey75", "firebrick")) + 
  labs(
    title = "Gene expression changes after traumatic brain injury",
    x = "log2 fold change (TBI vs sham)",
    y = "-log10 adjusted p-value",
    colour = "Significant and |LFC| > 1"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

# look at the plot

newvolcano
```

### Question 3

```{r}
# overwrite our volcano object with some more geoms
newvolcano <- newvolcano +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), 
                 linetype = "dashed", 
                 colour = "black") + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), 
                 linetype = "dashed", 
                 colour = "black") # notice here we create a vector of x intercepts using c() so that we can have more than one x intercept


# look at the plot 
newvolcano
```
